summary: Defines a MIME content type for Message Disposition Notifications, which report what happened to a message after delivery, such as read receipts. It also defines headers for requesting them. It obsoletes RFC 2298, updates RFC 2046 and RFC 3461, was updated by RFC 5337 and RFC 6533, and was replaced by RFC 8098.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines a small machine-readable report that a mail program can send back to say what it did with a message, such as displaying it or deleting it. The sender has to ask for the report with a header, and the recipient's program is free to refuse.

questions: what is a message disposition notification
how do email read receipts work
can a recipient refuse a read receipt
subtitle: How a mail system tells the sender what happened to a message after it was delivered.

tldr.problem: Senders of mail had no way to learn what happened to a message after it was delivered, and the read receipts offered by other messaging systems had no standard form on the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a MIME content type, message/disposition-notification, carried inside a multipart/report, plus the Disposition-Notification-To header that asks a recipient's mail program to send one.
tldr.outcome: The RFC was a standards-track specification that obsoleted RFC 2298, and the RFC Editor index lists it as obsoleted by RFC 8098. It was later updated by RFC 5337 and RFC 6533.

today: RFC 3798 is a May 2004 standards-track memo, and the RFC Editor index lists it as obsoleted by RFC 8098. It was later updated by RFC 5337 and RFC 6533.

sections.title: What a Message Disposition Notification Is
sections.content:
The RFC defines a MIME content type that a mail user agent or electronic mail gateway can use to report the disposition of a message after it has been successfully delivered to a recipient. The content type is intended to be machine-processable, and additional message headers are defined so that a sender can ask for disposition notifications. The purpose is to extend Internet mail with functionality often found in other messaging systems, such as X.400 and the proprietary LAN-based systems, and often referred to as read receipts, acknowledgements or receipt notifications, while respecting the privacy concerns that have often been expressed when such functions are discussed.

Because many messages are sent between the Internet and other messaging systems, the protocol is designed to be useful in a multi-protocol environment. It provides for the carriage of foreign addresses in addition to those normally used in Internet mail, and additional attributes may be defined to support tunnelling of foreign notifications through Internet mail.

The notifications are expected to serve several purposes: to inform people of the disposition of messages after successful delivery in a way that does not depend on human language; to let mail user agents keep track of the disposition of messages they sent, by associating returned notifications with earlier transmissions; to convey disposition notification requests and notifications between Internet mail and foreign mail systems through a gateway; to let foreign notifications be tunnelled through a MIME-capable message system and back into the system that issued them, or even into a third system; and to give language-independent but reasonably precise indications of what happened to a message.

Those purposes place four constraints on the protocol. It must be readable by humans and machine-parsable. It must carry enough information for a sender to link a notification unambiguously to the message that was sent and the original recipient address, even if the message was forwarded. It must be able to describe the disposition of a message independently of any human language or of the terminology of any particular mail system. And the specification must be extensible.
sections.plainLanguage: A disposition notification is a small report that comes back to the sender saying what the recipient's mail program did with the message. The RFC wants it to be readable by a person and by a program, to travel safely between different mail systems, and to leave room for new fields later.

sections.title: Requesting a Notification
sections.content:
Notifications are requested by including a Disposition-Notification-To header in the message, whose syntax is a header name followed by one or more mailboxes separated by commas. The presence of the header is merely a request, and the recipient's user agents are always free to silently ignore it. Alternatively, an explicit denial can be sent using the denied disposition in a notification. A notification must not itself have a Disposition-Notification-To header, and a notification must not be generated in response to a notification.

A user agent must not issue more than one notification on behalf of each particular recipient, so once one has been issued for a recipient, no further ones may be issued for that recipient even if another disposition is performed on the message. If a message is forwarded, a notification may have been issued for the recipient doing the forwarding, and the recipient of the forwarded message may also cause one to be generated. Because Internet standards normally do not specify the behaviour of user interfaces, it is strongly recommended that the user agent obtain the user's consent before sending a notification, either per message through a prompt or globally through a preference. The user might also indicate globally that notifications are never to be sent, or that a denied notification is always sent in response to a request.

Notifications should not be sent automatically if the address in the Disposition-Notification-To header differs from the address in the Return-Path header, and in that case confirmation from the user should be obtained if possible; if consent cannot be obtained, no notification should be sent. Confirmation should also be obtained, or no notification sent, if there is no Return-Path header, or if there is more than one distinct address in the Disposition-Notification-To header. Addresses are compared using only the addr-spec portion, excluding any phrase and route, and the comparison must be case-sensitive for the local part and case-insensitive for the domain. The reason for not sending automatically in these cases is to reduce the possibility of mail loops and of notifications being used for mail bombing.

A message with a Disposition-Notification-To header should also contain a Message-ID header, so that notifications can be correlated with their original messages automatically. If a request is wanted for some recipients and not others, two copies of the message should be sent, one with the header and one without, and the recipients in the respective envelopes decide for whom notifications are requested. Messages posted to newsgroups should not have the header.

Two further headers carry information for the recipient's program. The Disposition-Notification-Options header provides an extensible mechanism for extra parameters, each written as an attribute, an importance of required or optional, and a value. If an important parameter is not understood, the program must not generate a notification with any disposition type other than failed. No parameters are defined in this specification, and names beginning with X- are reserved for experimental use. The Original-Recipient header lets the delivering mail transfer agent pass on the recipient address the sender specified, which the delivery status notification extension of SMTP can supply, so that notifications can be correlated on a per recipient basis.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender asks for a notification with a header naming where to send it, and the recipient's program may ignore the request, ask the user, or send a refusal. The rules are strict about one notification per recipient, and about not sending one automatically to an address that differs from the envelope sender, because that is how a flood could be aimed at someone else.

sections.title: The Format of a Notification
sections.content:
A notification is a MIME message whose top-level content type is multipart/report. The report-type parameter of that multipart content is disposition-notification. The first component of the multipart contains a human-readable explanation of the notification. The second component is of content type message/disposition-notification. If the original message or a portion of it is to be returned to the sender, it appears as the third component, and it is up to the generating program whether to return it, except that encrypted message text must be returned, if at all, only in its original encrypted form.

The notification must be addressed, in both the message header and the transport envelope, to the address from the Disposition-Notification-To header of the original message for which the notification is being generated. The From field must contain the address of the person for whom the notification is issued, and the envelope sender address of the notification must be null, so that no delivery status notifications are sent in response to a notification. The Message-ID header, if present, must differ from the Message-ID of the message for which the notification is issued, and a particular notification describes the disposition of exactly one message for exactly one recipient.

The message/disposition-notification content type has MIME type name message, subtype disposition-notification, no optional parameters, and 7bit encoding, which is sufficient and must be used to keep the content readable to mail readers that do not understand MIME. The body consists of one or more fields. In order they may be the Reporting-UA field, naming the program that performed the disposition, the MDN-Gateway field, naming the gateway that translated a foreign notification, the Original-Recipient field, the Final-Recipient field, which must be present, the Original-Message-ID field, which must be present if the original message had a Message-ID, the Disposition field, which must be present, and then any number of failure, error and warning fields and extension fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The notification is a MIME message with two parts: a human-readable explanation and a machine-readable block of fields. The machine-readable part names the program that reported, the original and final recipients, the identifier of the original message, and what was done with it.

sections.title: The Disposition Field and Its Values
sections.content:
The Disposition field says what the reporting program did on behalf of the user, and it is made of a mode and a type, with optional modifiers. The mode has two halves. The action mode is manual-action, when the disposition was the result of an explicit instruction by the user, or automatic-action, when it was the result of an automatic action; one or the other must be given. The sending mode is MDN-sent-manually, when the user explicitly gave permission for this particular notification to be sent, or MDN-sent-automatically, when the program had been configured to send it automatically; again one or the other must be given.

The disposition type is displayed, meaning the message has been displayed by the program to someone reading the recipient's mailbox, with no guarantee that the content has been read or understood, or deleted, meaning the message has been deleted and the recipient may or may not have seen it, and might undelete it and read it later. A disposition modifier may follow, of which only the extension modifier is defined, so that modifiers can be added by later revisions. Names beginning with X- are reserved for experimental use, and other names must be registered with IANA. A notification with a modifier name that the receiving program does not understand may be silently ignored or filed in the mailbox without special interpretation, and it must not cause any error message to be sent to the sender. A program is not required to be able to generate all of the possible values of the field.

The Failure, Error and Warning fields supply additional text when the failure disposition type, the error disposition modifier and the warning disposition modifier appear. The Reporting-UA field is optional but recommended, and for Internet mail user agents it is recommended that it hold both the DNS name of the particular instance of the program and the name of the product, for example pc.example.com; Foomail 97.1. The MDN-Gateway field must appear in any notification that a gateway translated from a foreign system, and must not appear otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: The Disposition field has two parts: how the message was handled and whether the user agreed. The type is either displayed or deleted. A program that meets a modifier it does not understand should not treat the notification as an error.

sections.title: When a Notification Is Generated
sections.content:
The RFC gives a timeline of the events in processing a message and generating notifications. The user composes the message and tells the program to send it, and the program passes it to the mail transfer agent along with the original recipient information. The agent sends the message to the next agent, the final agent receives it, and the final agent delivers it to the user agent, possibly generating a delivery status notification. The user agent then performs automatic processing and generates corresponding notifications, with the dispatched, processed, deleted, denied or failed disposition type and the automatic-action and MDN-sent-automatically modes.

The user agent then shows the list of messages to the user, who selects a message and asks for an action to be performed on it. The program performs the requested action and, with the user's permission, sends an appropriate notification, with the displayed, dispatched, processed, deleted, denied or failed disposition type and the manual-action mode. The user may perform other actions on the message afterwards, but no further notifications are generated.

On conformance, a user agent or gateway conforms to the specification if it generates notifications according to the protocol, and it is not necessary to be able to generate all of the possible values of the Disposition field. A user agent or gateway must not generate the Original-Recipient field unless the mail protocols provide the address originally specified by the sender at the time of submission, which ordinary SMTP does not guarantee. Successful distribution of a message to a mailing list exploder should be considered the final disposition of the message, and the exploder may issue a notification with the processed disposition type, but propagating the request to all the members of the list is not recommended for anything but small, closely knit lists, because it might cause large numbers of notifications and may reveal confidential subscribers.
sections.plainLanguage: A program can report something the moment it handles a message, or later when the person asks it to do something. Either way, one message and one recipient produce one notification, and that is the end of it for that recipient.

sections.title: Forgery, Privacy and Mail Bombing
sections.content:
Notifications may be forged as easily as ordinary Internet electronic mail, so user agents and automatic mail handling facilities that make automatic use of them should take precautions against denial-of-service attacks. The threats include a falsified notification sent when the disposition never happened, and unsolicited notifications.

Privacy is the other dimension. A recipient may not wish the disposition of messages addressed to him to be known, or may be concerned that sending a notification reveals sensitive information, such as when the message was read. In that situation it is acceptable for the program to issue a denied notification or to ignore the request silently. If the Disposition-Notification-To header is passed on unmodified when a message is distributed to a mailing list, the subscribers to the list may be revealed to the sender of the original message. Headers of the original message returned in the third part of the multipart report could reveal confidential information about host names and network topology inside a firewall, and an unencrypted notification could reveal information about an encrypted message.

Notifications do not provide non-repudiation with proof of delivery. They give the mail user valuable information, but they cannot be relied upon as a guarantee that a message was or was not seen by the recipient, since they may be lost in transit and the recipient may bypass the mechanism entirely. The RFC points to RFC 2634 as one possible solution for that purpose.

The request mechanism also introduces a new way of mail-bombing a mailbox. An attacking agent can send a large set of messages to unsuspecting third parties with a false disposition-notification-to address, and automatic or simplistic processing would flood the target of the attack with notifications, overrunning the mailbox and denying service. For that reason notifications should not be sent automatically where the disposition-notification-to address is different from the envelope MAIL FROM address.
sections.plainLanguage: A notification can be faked, so treat one as a claim rather than a fact. It can also leak information about the recipient, and a wrong request address can be used to flood someone else's mailbox with replies.

viz.caption: THE VALUES OF THE DISPOSITION FIELD

items.label: Manual action
items.desc: The disposition came from an explicit instruction by the user.

items.label: Automatic action
items.desc: The disposition came from an automatic action, not from an instruction.

items.label: Sent with permission
items.desc: The user explicitly gave permission for this notification to be sent.

items.label: Sent automatically
items.desc: The program had been configured to send notifications automatically.

items.label: Displayed
items.desc: The message was shown to someone reading the mailbox; it may not have been read.

items.label: Deleted
items.desc: The message was deleted; the recipient may or may not have seen it.
